---
title: "About"
---

## What this is

A benchmark of **performance**, not answer quality. The tasks these models are
given exist only to consume and generate tokens; nothing here evaluates whether
the output is any good. The question is narrower and less often answered
honestly: push a runtime's tuning parameters to their limit, and what can this
hardware really do?

## The test bench

Every published number comes from one machine:

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | Intel Core Ultra 7, 20 cores |
| RAM | 64 GB DDR5 |
| GPU | NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti, 16 GB (Blackwell, ~448 GB/s, 128-bit bus) |

Results are labelled with a **hardware profile**, and the claim is verified
against the box in software before a run starts — a mismatch is an error, not a
footnote:

- **budget** — "everybody's computer": 1× RTX 5060 Ti, 32 GB RAM (capped with a
  cgroup on the larger box). This is what ships today.
- **enthusiast** — 2× RTX 5060 Ti (32 GB VRAM), 64 GB RAM. Waiting on a second
  card.

## What gets measured

| Metric | Definition |
|---|---|
| Prompt processing (prefill) | prompt tokens / prefill time, as a function of prompt length |
| Time-to-first-token | request sent → first token received, client-side, streaming |
| Decode speed | generated tokens/s single-stream, as a function of context depth — the curve, not one number |
| Max context | the largest context that loads **and** completes a full-context request without running out of memory, plus the speed at that limit |
| Batched throughput | total tokens/s and latency percentiles against concurrency |
| VRAM | peak, per configuration, via NVML |
| Power | via NVML, integrated to energy per token |
| Load time | cold start → server ready |

## How the numbers are produced

A parameter sweep runs as a staged funnel: a cheap coarse grid ranks
configurations, the leaders get a denser grid, and a handful of finalists get
the full treatment — long contexts, complete curves, repeated runs. Some
parameters barely matter at small scale and dominate at large scale
(flash-attention is the clearest case), so those dimensions are never pruned
early.

Objectives conflict — maximum context, maximum throughput and minimum latency
are usually different configurations — so results are published per objective
instead of collapsing into one "best".

Practices that make the numbers worth reading: warmup runs before measurement,
several repetitions with the median and spread reported rather than a single
figure, cooldown between heavy runs because thermals are real, exact token
counts cut with the model's own tokenizer, forced output lengths so every
configuration generates exactly the same number of tokens, and pinned runtime
versions recorded with every result. Out-of-memory outcomes are recorded as
data — they are where the boundary is.

## How posts get here

Articles are generated by a private pipeline from committed results and arrive
as pull requests, charts included. A human reads, edits and merges; the merge is
what publishes. The commentary is written by hand, the numbers never are.

Posts are syndicated to dev.to with the canonical link pointing back here.
